blocks.robotComment: Every website you've ever visited is built on this one idea. 🌐
blocks.body: HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language. It is not a programming language in the traditional sense — it does not calculate, loop, or make decisions. Instead, it describes the structure and content of a web page: which piece of text is a heading, which is a paragraph, which is a link.

highlights.text: it describes the structure and content of a web page

code.caption: HTML labels content with tags — here, a big heading and a paragraph.

blocks.body: "Markup" means exactly that: you take plain text and mark it up with tags that say what each piece is. A browser reads those tags and displays the content accordingly — a heading looks big and bold, a paragraph wraps normally, a link is clickable.

highlights.text: you take plain text and mark it up with tags that say what each piece is

blocks.body: Every website you've ever visited — no matter what it's built with underneath — sends HTML to your browser in the end. Frameworks and backend languages generate it, content management systems assemble it, but HTML is always the actual thing the browser receives and renders.

highlights.text: HTML is always the actual thing the browser receives and renders

blocks.question: What does HTML actually do?
options: It describes the structure and content of a web page using tags
It performs calculations and makes logical decisions
It stores data in a database
It compiles into machine code before running
blocks.explanation: HTML marks up content to describe its structure — headings, paragraphs, links — it does not calculate or make decisions.
HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language.

blocks.statement: HTML is a programming language that can perform calculations and loops.
blocks.explanation: HTML is a markup language, not a programming language — it describes structure and content, not logic.

blocks.body: HTML was created in 1991 by Tim Berners-Lee, a researcher at CERN, as a way to link scientific documents together so people could jump between related papers by clicking. That original version had only about 18 tags.

highlights.text: a way to link scientific documents together so people could jump between related papers by clicking

blocks.robotComment: From 18 tags to an entire web platform. Not bad for one researcher. 📜
blocks.body: Through the 1990s, HTML went through several versions as more browsers and companies got involved, each adding new tags for things like tables, forms, and images. This period was messy — different browsers supported different tags, and pages often looked different depending on which browser opened them.

highlights.text: different browsers supported different tags, and pages often looked different depending on which browser opened them

blocks.body: HTML5, released in 2014, is the version this track teaches and the one every modern browser supports today. It added semantic tags (which describe meaning, not just appearance), native support for audio and video, and cleaned up a lot of the inconsistency from earlier versions.

highlights.text: It added semantic tags (which describe meaning, not just appearance), native support for audio and video

blocks.question: Who created HTML, and why?
options: Tim Berners-Lee, to link scientific documents together at CERN
A group of browser companies, to compete with each other
Oracle, to replace Java on the web
It was created specifically for mobile apps
blocks.explanation: Tim Berners-Lee created HTML in 1991 at CERN so researchers could link related documents together.

blocks.sentence: ___, released in 2014, is the version of HTML every modern browser supports today.
blocks.explanation: HTML5 was released in 2014 and is the current standard version taught in this track.

blocks.statement: The very first version of HTML in 1991 already had support for audio and video.
blocks.explanation: The original 1991 version had only about 18 basic tags — audio and video support came much later, with HTML5.

blocks.body: When a browser loads a web page, it reads the HTML from top to bottom and builds an internal model of it called the DOM — the Document Object Model. Every tag becomes a piece of that model, nested inside whichever tag contains it.

highlights.text: it reads the HTML from top to bottom and builds an internal model of it called the DOM

blocks.robotComment: The DOM is the browser's own mental map of your page. 🗺️
blocks.body: You don't write the DOM directly — you write HTML, and the browser constructs the DOM from it as it reads. This is worth knowing now because later tracks (like JavaScript) interact with the DOM directly to change a page after it's loaded, and none of that makes sense without first understanding that HTML becomes the DOM.

highlights.text: you write HTML, and the browser constructs the DOM from it as it reads

blocks.body: The browser is also forgiving. If you forget to close a tag or make a small mistake, most browsers will guess what you meant and display something anyway, rather than refusing to show the page at all. That's convenient, but it also means broken HTML can look fine by accident — this track will teach you to write it correctly from the start.

highlights.text: broken HTML can look fine by accident — this track will teach you to write it correctly from the start

blocks.question: What does a browser build from HTML as it reads a page?
options: The DOM (Document Object Model) — its internal model of the page
A database of the page contents
Nothing — it displays the raw HTML text as-is
blocks.explanation: The browser reads HTML top to bottom and builds the DOM, its internal model of the page structure.

blocks.sentence: The browser's internal model of a page, built from HTML, is called the ___.
blocks.explanation: DOM stands for Document Object Model — the browser's internal representation of the page.

blocks.statement: Browsers always refuse to display a page at all if the HTML has any small mistake in it.
blocks.explanation: Browsers are forgiving — they typically guess at broken HTML and display something anyway, rather than refusing entirely.

blocks.body: Web pages are usually described as three separate layers working together: HTML for structure and content, CSS for visual styling (colors, layout, fonts), and JavaScript for behavior and interactivity. This track covers only the first one.

highlights.text: HTML for structure and content, CSS for visual styling (colors, layout, fonts), and JavaScript for behavior and interactivity

blocks.robotComment: Structure first. Everything else builds on top of it. 🏗️
blocks.body: A useful comparison: HTML is like a building's frame and rooms — where the walls are, what each room is for. CSS is the paint, furniture, and lighting. JavaScript is the plumbing and electrical systems that make things actually respond and function. You can have a frame with no paint, but you can't paint a building that doesn't exist yet.

highlights.text: you can't paint a building that doesn't exist yet

blocks.body: This is exactly why HTML comes first. Every other web skill — styling with CSS, adding interactivity with JavaScript (already a track in this app) — assumes there's already a page structure to style or manipulate. Solid HTML is the foundation everything else in web development sits on.

highlights.text: Solid HTML is the foundation everything else in web development sits on

blocks.question: In the three-layer model of a web page, what is HTML responsible for?
options: Visual styling like colors and layout
blocks.explanation: HTML handles structure and content; CSS handles visual styling; JavaScript handles behavior and interactivity.

blocks.sentence: ___ is responsible for a web page's visual styling, like colors, layout, and fonts.
blocks.explanation: CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) handles visual styling, separate from HTML's structure and content.

blocks.statement: CSS and JavaScript can style and add behavior to a page without any HTML structure existing first.
blocks.explanation: CSS and JavaScript both act on HTML structure that already exists — there has to be a page to style or manipulate first.

chapters.title: The Shape of an HTML Document

blocks.body: Every HTML document starts with a doctype declaration — a single line that tells the browser which version of HTML the page is written in, so it knows how to interpret everything that follows.

highlights.text: tells the browser which version of HTML the page is written in

code.caption: The complete HTML5 doctype — short, and always exactly this line.

blocks.robotComment: Older doctypes were long, ugly, and easy to typo. HTML5 fixed that. 🎉
blocks.body: Older versions of HTML had long, awkward doctype declarations full of version numbers and URLs. HTML5 simplified this dramatically — the line above is the entire doctype, and it never changes from page to page.

highlights.text: the line above is the entire doctype, and it never changes from page to page

blocks.body: Without a doctype, browsers fall back to something called 'quirks mode,' where they guess at older, inconsistent rendering behavior to stay compatible with very old pages. That's rarely what you want, so the doctype always belongs at the very top of every HTML file, before anything else.

highlights.text: the doctype always belongs at the very top of every HTML file, before anything else

blocks.question: What is the correct HTML5 doctype declaration?
options: Exactly what is shown — a short, unchanging line
There is no doctype in HTML5 — it was removed
blocks.explanation: The HTML5 doctype is simply <!DOCTYPE html> — short and identical on every page.

blocks.sentence: Without a doctype, browsers may fall back to ___ mode, guessing at older rendering behavior.
blocks.explanation: Missing a doctype can trigger "quirks mode," where the browser guesses at old, inconsistent rendering rules.

blocks.statement: The doctype declaration should be placed at the very top of an HTML file, before anything else.
blocks.explanation: The doctype always goes first, before the <html> tag or anything else in the file.

lessons.title: The html, head, and body Elements

blocks.body: Right after the doctype, every HTML document has one <html> element that wraps everything else, and inside it exactly two direct children: <head> and <body>.

highlights.text: exactly two direct children: <head> and <body>

code.code:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
  <head>
    <!-- page info goes here -->
  </head>
  <body>
    <!-- visible content goes here -->
  </body>
</html>
code.caption: The complete skeleton every HTML page starts from.

blocks.robotComment: Head is for the browser and search engines. Body is for the person looking at the screen. 👀
blocks.body: The <head> holds information about the page that is not directly displayed on the screen — things like the page title, character encoding, and links to other files. The <body> holds everything a visitor actually sees: text, images, buttons, links, all of it.

highlights.text: The <head> holds information about the page that is not directly displayed on the screen

blocks.body: A common beginner mistake is putting visible content in the <head> by accident, or forgetting the <body> tag entirely. Browsers are forgiving enough to often still show something, but relying on that guesswork is a habit worth avoiding from the start.

highlights.text: A common beginner mistake is putting visible content in the <head> by accident

blocks.question: What are the two direct children of the <html> element?
blocks.explanation: Every HTML document's <html> element contains exactly a <head> and a <body>.

blocks.sentence: The ___ element holds everything a visitor actually sees on the page — text, images, buttons, and links.
blocks.explanation: The <body> element contains all the visible content of the page.

blocks.statement: The <head> element is where visible page content like paragraphs and images belongs.
blocks.explanation: Visible content belongs in <body> — <head> holds non-visible page information like the title and metadata.

blocks.body:
Three terms get used constantly in HTML, and it's worth being precise about them. A tag is the actual markup, like

or

. An element is a tag together with its content — the opening tag, everything inside, and the closing tag. An attribute is extra information added inside an opening tag.

highlights.text: An element is a tag together with its content — the opening tag, everything inside, and the closing tag

code.caption: and are tags. The whole thing together is an element. href="https://example.com" is an attribute.

blocks.robotComment: Attributes are how a tag says "and here's a detail about me." 🏷️
blocks.body: An attribute always lives inside the opening tag, written as a name, an equals sign, and a value in quotes: name="value". A single tag can carry several attributes, separated by spaces.

highlights.text: a name, an equals sign, and a value in quotes: name="value"

code.caption: Three attributes on one tag: src, alt, and width.

blocks.body: These words get used loosely in everyday conversation — people often say 'tag' when they mean 'element,' and that's fine informally. But knowing the precise difference will make documentation and error messages far easier to understand as this track goes on.

highlights.text: knowing the precise difference will make documentation and error messages far easier to understand

blocks.question: In Click here, what is href="https://example.com"?
blocks.explanation: href="https://example.com" is an attribute — extra information added inside the opening tag.

blocks.sentence: A(n) ___ is a tag together with everything inside it, from the opening tag to the closing tag.
blocks.explanation: An element is the full package: opening tag, content, and closing tag together.

blocks.statement: A single tag can only ever have one attribute.
blocks.explanation: A tag can carry several attributes at once, separated by spaces.

blocks.body:
Most HTML tags come in pairs: an opening tag like

and a matching closing tag like

, with content sandwiched between them. The closing tag is identical to the opening one except for the forward slash right after the <.

highlights.text:
an opening tag like

and a matching closing tag like

code.caption: An opening tag, some content, and a matching closing tag.

blocks.robotComment: No content, no closing tag needed — the tag says everything on its own. ✅
blocks.body:
Some tags never wrap content at all, so they have no separate closing tag — they're called self-closing (or void) elements. ,

highlights.text: they're called self-closing (or void) elements

code.caption: Neither of these tags has, or needs, a closing tag.

blocks.body: Forgetting a closing tag on a paired element is one of the most common beginner mistakes, and it's often the cause of a page looking subtly broken — content nested in the wrong place, or formatting bleeding further than intended. Getting into the habit of closing every paired tag prevents most of these bugs before they happen.

highlights.text: Forgetting a closing tag on a paired element is one of the most common beginner mistakes

blocks.question: Which of these is a self-closing (void) element that never needs a closing tag?
blocks.explanation: is a void element — it never wraps content, so it has no closing tag.

blocks.sentence: A closing tag is written the same as an opening tag, but with a forward ___ right after the <.
blocks.explanation:
Closing tags add a forward slash right after the <, like

.

blocks.statement: Every single HTML tag requires a matching closing tag.
blocks.explanation:
Void elements like and
never wrap content, so they have no closing tag at all.

blocks.body: Elements can contain other elements, and this is called nesting. The rule is simple but important: whichever element you open last must be the one you close first — nested tags have to close in the reverse order they opened.

highlights.text: whichever element you open last must be the one you close first

code.caption:
opens after

and closes before

— correctly nested.

blocks.robotComment: Crossed tags are the HTML equivalent of tangled shoelaces. 👟
blocks.body: Tags that cross each other instead of nesting properly are invalid and can cause a browser to render the page in unexpected ways, even if it technically still displays something.

highlights.text: Tags that cross each other instead of nesting properly are invalid

code.caption:
Invalid — opened after

but closes after

instead of before it.

blocks.body: A good habit for avoiding nesting mistakes is indenting nested elements consistently as you write them, the way the examples in this track do. It costs nothing and makes crossed or missing tags far easier to spot at a glance, especially once a page has dozens of elements in it.

highlights.text: indenting nested elements consistently as you write them

blocks.question: What is the correct rule for closing nested HTML tags?
options: Whichever element you opened last must be the one you close first
Tags can be closed in any order at all
Only the outermost tag ever needs a closing tag
Closing order does not matter as long as every tag eventually closes
blocks.explanation: Nested tags must close in the reverse order they opened — last opened, first closed.

blocks.sentence: Elements containing other elements is called ___.
blocks.explanation: Putting elements inside other elements is called nesting.

This is invalid — the tags cross instead of nesting; should close before

, not after.

blocks.body: HTML comments let you leave notes in your code that browsers completely ignore when rendering the page. They start with <!-- and end with -->, and anything in between is invisible to visitors.

highlights.text: They start with <!-- and end with -->, and anything in between is invisible to visitors

code.code: Home
code.caption: The comment explains the section below it, but never appears on the page itself.

blocks.robotComment: Comments are for future-you, and for anyone else reading your code later. 📝
blocks.body: Comments are useful for labeling sections of a longer page ('this is the header,' 'this is the footer'), leaving reminders about something that needs fixing later, or temporarily disabling a piece of HTML without deleting it while testing.

highlights.text: labeling sections of a longer page

blocks.body: One thing worth knowing: HTML comments are not truly hidden. Anyone can view a page's source code and read every comment in it. Never put anything sensitive — passwords, private notes, internal-only information — inside an HTML comment.

highlights.text: Anyone can view a page's source code and read every comment in it

blocks.question: How does an HTML comment begin and end?
options: Begins with // and ends with a line break
Begins with # and has no ending
blocks.explanation: HTML comments always start with <!-- and end with -->.

blocks.sentence: Content inside an HTML comment is invisible on the rendered page, but anyone can still see it by viewing the page ___.
blocks.explanation: Comments never render, but anyone viewing the page source can still read them.

blocks.statement: It is safe to put a password or private note inside an HTML comment, since browsers never display it.
blocks.explanation: Comments are invisible on the rendered page but fully visible in the page source — never put sensitive information in one.

blocks.body: HTML gives you six levels of heading, <h1> through <h6>, each one marking a title or section header. <h1> is the most important heading on the page and <h6> the least important — browsers shrink the default font size as the number climbs, but the real point of headings is to build a hierarchy, like the outline of a document, not just to make text bigger or bolder.

highlights.text: the real point of headings is to build a hierarchy, like the outline of a document, not just to make text bigger or bolder

code.caption: Three heading levels, each one step deeper into the page's structure.

blocks.robotComment: Headings aren't just big text — they're a map of the page. 🗺️
blocks.body: Screen readers let users jump straight from heading to heading to skim a page, and search engines use headings to figure out what a page is actually about. Both depend on the heading levels reflecting real structure, not just how someone wanted the text to look.

highlights.text: Screen readers let users jump straight from heading to heading to skim a page

blocks.body: Every heading level comes with a default size and weight baked into the browser, but that's just a starting point — real projects almost always override it with CSS. Pick a heading level for what it means in the outline, not for how big or bold it happens to look by default.

highlights.text: Pick a heading level for what it means in the outline, not for how big or bold it happens to look by default

code.caption: Even shrunk with CSS, this is still an <h1> as far as the page's structure is concerned.

blocks.question: What is the actual purpose of heading levels like <h1> through <h6>?
options: To build a hierarchy that reflects the page's structure
To make certain text bigger on the screen
blocks.explanation: Headings exist to describe structure — an outline screen readers and search engines can rely on — not just to control font size.

blocks.sentence: The most important heading on a page, typically used once near the top, is ___.
blocks.explanation: <h1> marks the single most important heading — the top of the page's outline.

blocks.statement: You should choose a heading level based on how big or bold you want the text to appear.
blocks.explanation: Heading levels should reflect the structure of the content. Visual size is a CSS concern, not a reason to pick a heading level.

blocks.body: A page should have exactly one <h1>, and it should describe what the whole page is about — think of it as the title of the document, the same way a book has one title even though it has many chapter headings inside it.

highlights.text: A page should have exactly one <h1>, and it should describe what the whole page is about

code.caption: One <h1> for the page, then <h2>s for its main sections.

blocks.robotComment: Two h1s is like a book with two titles on the cover. 📖
blocks.body: Stuffing a page with several <h1> tags — one per section, say — breaks the outline that screen readers and search engines build from your headings. Instead of one clear topic, they see several competing 'most important' headings and have no way to tell which one the page is really about.

highlights.text: breaks the outline that screen readers and search engines build from your headings

blocks.body: This isn't a hard rule enforced by browsers — a page with three <h1> tags will still render just fine. It's a convention that keeps a page's structure meaningful, the same way a well-organized document only ever has one main title even if it has many sections underneath it.

highlights.text: a page with three <h1> tags will still render just fine

blocks.question: Why should a page normally have only one <h1>?
options: It represents the single main topic of the page, like a document title
Browsers refuse to render a second <h1>
Only one <h1> is allowed per website, not per page
<h1> can only be used inside the <head>
blocks.explanation: The <h1> is meant to represent the page's single main topic — like a book's title, not one of its chapter headings.

blocks.statement: A browser will refuse to display a page that contains more than one <h1> element.
blocks.explanation: Browsers render multiple <h1> tags without complaint — one-per-page is a structural convention, not a technical restriction.

blocks.sentence: Using several <h1> tags on one page confuses the ___ that screen readers and search engines build from your headings.
blocks.explanation: Multiple <h1>s give screen readers and search engines several competing "main" headings instead of one clear outline.

blocks.body: Headings should nest in order, one level at a time: <h1>, then <h2> for its main sections, then <h3> for subsections inside those, and so on. Skipping a level — going straight from <h1> to <h3> — is a common mistake that leaves a gap in the outline.

highlights.text: Headings should nest in order, one level at a time

code.caption: Correct nesting — no level is skipped, and the structure is easy to follow.

blocks.robotComment: Skipping from h1 to h3 leaves a hole where h2 should be. 🕳️
blocks.body: Jumping straight from <h1> to <h3> doesn't just look inconsistent — it actively breaks the outline a screen reader user relies on to navigate the page, since they land on an <h3> with no <h2> above it to explain what section they are even in.

highlights.text: actively breaks the outline a screen reader user relies on to navigate the page

code.caption: Broken nesting — this <h3> skipped right over <h2>, leaving a gap in the outline.

blocks.body: It's fine to go back up — an <h2> can follow an <h3> once you start a new section, the same way a book can move from a subsection back to a new chapter. What you want to avoid is skipping downward past a level on the way in.

highlights.text: It's fine to go back up

blocks.question: Which of these heading sequences is correctly nested?
blocks.explanation: Going down one level at a time, and stepping back up to start a new section, keeps the outline intact.

blocks.statement: Jumping directly from an <h1> to an <h3>, with no <h2> in between, is good practice.
blocks.explanation: Skipping a heading level leaves a gap in the page outline, which is confusing for screen reader users in particular.

blocks.sentence: After using an <h3> for a subsection, starting a brand-new main section should go back ___ to <h2>, not stay at <h3>.
blocks.explanation: Stepping back up to a higher-level heading to start a new section keeps the outline logical.

lessons.title: Strong vs. Bold: Meaning vs. Look

blocks.body: Both <strong> and <b> make text render bold by default, but they mean different things. <strong> marks text as important — content the reader genuinely should not miss, like a warning. <b> just makes text visually bold, with no claim about how important it is.

highlights.text: <strong> marks text as important
<b> just makes text visually bold, with no claim about how important it is

code.code:
Warning: unsaved changes will be lost.

The report's Q3 figures are on page 4.
code.caption: Both render bold in a browser, but only the first one is marked as actually important.

blocks.robotComment: Same look, different message — one is a shout, the other is just a font choice. 📢
blocks.body: This difference is invisible to the eye but not to assistive technology: a screen reader can announce <strong> text with added emphasis in its voice, and search engines may give slightly more weight to text marked as important. <b> carries none of that — it is purely a visual style.

highlights.text: a screen reader can announce <strong> text with added emphasis in its voice

blocks.body: A good rule of thumb: reach for <strong> when you would say the words louder if reading the page out loud — a warning, a key term, a critical instruction. Reach for <b> when you just want something to stand out visually, like a product name in a list, with no real urgency behind it.

highlights.text: reach for <strong> when you would say the words louder if reading the page out loud

blocks.question: What is the key difference between <strong> and <b>?
options: <strong> carries semantic importance, while <b> is purely visual
<strong> makes text italic, <b> makes text bold
There is no difference — they are interchangeable
blocks.explanation: <strong> tells assistive tools and search engines that content is important; <b> only affects appearance.

blocks.statement: A screen reader treats <strong> text exactly the same as <b> text, since they look identical in a browser.
blocks.explanation: Screen readers can add emphasis when announcing <strong> text, because it carries semantic meaning that <b> does not.

blocks.sentence: Use ___ when text is genuinely important, and reserve <b> for text that should just look bold with no real significance.
blocks.explanation: <strong> is the semantically correct choice for text that actually matters, not just text you want to look bold.

lessons.title: Emphasis vs. Italic: Meaning vs. Look

blocks.body: <em> and <i> both render as italic text by default, and they follow the same pattern as <strong> and <b>: <em> means stress emphasis — it actually changes how a sentence should be read — while <i> is a purely visual style with no semantic weight.

highlights.text: <em> means stress emphasis — it actually changes how a sentence should be read
<i> is a purely visual style with no semantic weight

code.code:
I did send the invoice.

The ship was named the Nautilus.
code.caption: The first <em> changes the sentence's meaning if read aloud; the <i> is just a styling convention for a name.

blocks.robotComment: Try reading a sentence with vocal stress on the <em> word — the meaning shifts. 🎙️
blocks.body: <em> is for the word or phrase a speaker would naturally stress out loud — "I did send the invoice" means something different depending on which word gets the emphasis. <i> is for text set apart by convention, like foreign words, technical terms, or the names of ships and books, where there is no vocal stress implied at all.

highlights.text: <i> is for text set apart by convention, like foreign words, technical terms, or the names of ships and books

code.code: The word schadenfreude has no direct English equivalent.
code.caption: A foreign term set in italics by convention — no emphasis is implied.

blocks.body: Screen readers can change their tone of voice for <em> text to reflect the added stress, the same way they can for <strong>. <i> text, like <b>, is announced no differently from regular text — it is a look, not a meaning.

highlights.text: Screen readers can change their tone of voice for <em> text to reflect the added stress

blocks.question: Which of these is the correct use of <em>?
options: Stressing a word that changes how a sentence should be read aloud
Styling a book title in italics with no vocal stress
blocks.explanation: <em> is for genuine stress emphasis — the kind that would change how you read a sentence out loud.

blocks.sentence: Setting a foreign word or a ship's name in italics with no vocal stress implied calls for ___, not <em>.
blocks.explanation: <i> is for text set apart by convention, without implying that it should be spoken with stress.

blocks.statement: <em> and <i> always mean exactly the same thing, just with different tag names.
blocks.explanation: <em> carries semantic stress emphasis, while <i> is a purely visual italic style with no semantic weight.

blocks.body: The <hr> element draws a horizontal line across the page. Visually it looks decorative, but its actual meaning is a thematic break — a signal that the content before it and the content after it are about a different topic.

highlights.text: its actual meaning is a thematic break

code.caption: The <hr> marks a shift between two unrelated sections of content.

blocks.robotComment: It's a semantic scene change, not just a decorative line. 🎬

code.caption: A complete, valid <hr> — nothing more is needed.

blocks.body: It's easy to reach for <hr> purely because a line looks nice between two sections, but that misses its purpose. Using it correctly — for an actual shift in topic — keeps the semantic meaning of your page intact for tools that rely on it, the same reasoning behind choosing <strong> over <b>.

highlights.text: Using it correctly — for an actual shift in topic — keeps the semantic meaning of your page intact

blocks.question: What does <hr> semantically represent, beyond just drawing a line?
options: A thematic break between two sections of content
A line break within one sentence
blocks.explanation: <hr> signals a shift in topic — the line is just the default visual representation of that break.
<hr> is a void element — it never wraps content, so it has no closing tag.

blocks.sentence: If you only want a decorative line with no real change of topic, that is better handled with ___ instead of <hr>.
blocks.explanation: <hr> carries semantic meaning about a topic shift — pure decoration belongs in CSS.
